title: Are Teaching and Learning Policies a Waste of Paper? 15, 2026
author: Adam Boxer
summary: Boxer opens with a school visit where a 48-page Teaching and Learning policy is not reflected in any observed lesson, a pattern he sees in most schools. He grants that aspirational policies and the reading behind them have value but argues they undermine leaders' standing, are best built collaboratively at department level, and carry a large opportunity cost compared with observing and coaching. As an alternative he proposes the rule 'Do We Do What We Say We Do?': observe lessons, keep what is both written and practised, remove what is not done, and rank the remaining practices on post-its as one-at-a-time targets. Each target is embedded before it re-enters the policy. He concludes that radical honesty and incremental improvement cut workload and raise motivation.
points: A policy that nobody follows erodes the credibility of those who wrote it and the culture of improvement.
Teachers and departments should build policy collaboratively, which also protects disciplinary integrity and ownership.
Leaders' time writing a policy is time not spent observing and giving feedback, and many leaders admit the latter would help more.
The post-it method sorts practices into done, not done and emergent, then embeds one priority at a time before adding it back to the policy.
quotes: If an organisation has a policy that nobody follows, then the standing of those responsible for that policy is undermined.
In addition, the act of contributing towards a policy like this increases your sense of ownership over it, and your drive to execute it properly.
Any time we spend on task x is time we could have spent on task y.
At our school, we always ask Do We Do What We Say We Do? It underpins everything about the school and what we do.
This keeps us relentlessly focused on the genuine lived experience of our students and colleagues as they are, not as we might wish them to be.
Once you’ve finished your observations, first consider the things that are both “in the policy and being done.” Celebrate success, and be proud of yourself and your colleagues.
In my experience being radically honest about your current practice, and committing to specific incremental improvements, delivers huge benefits in terms of staff workload, motivation, and practice.
